title: Laazim w mumkin — must, may, can
goal: Express obligation, permission, and ability — three ideas English blurs with "can," and Arabic keeps strictly apart.
bekal: tell apart لَازِم، مُمْكِن، فِيني، and بِقْدَر
ask permission and turn down requests politely
state obligations that apply to anyone

dialogs.title: حَكِي — بِمَكْتَب الْجَامْعَة
dialogs.intro: Budi is renewing his residence permit and asks a clerk at the university office.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Hello. May I ask about the residence permit?

lines.speaker: اَلْمُوَظَّف:
lines.id: Go ahead. What would you like to know?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: What do I need to bring?

lines.speaker: اَلْمُوَظَّف:
lines.baca: laazim tjiib jawaaz es-safar w ṣuurtēn.
lines.id: You need to bring your passport and two photos.

lines.speaker: اَلْمُوَظَّف:
lines.text: مُمْكِن، بَسّ لَازِم تِيجِي قَبِل الظُّهِر.
lines.id: Yes, but you have to come before noon.
lines.literal: possible, but must you-come before the-noon.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: مَا فِيني أَجِي بَعِد الظُّهِر؟ عِنْدِي صَفّ.
lines.baca: ma fiini aji ba‘d eḍ-ḍuhr? ‘indi ṣaff.
lines.id: Can't I come after noon? I have class.
lines.literal: not can-I I-come after the-noon? at-me class.

lines.speaker: اَلْمُوَظَّف:
lines.text: لَلْأَسَف لَا. اَلْمَكْتَب بْيِسَكِّر السَّاعَة وَحْدِة.
lines.baca: lal-asaf la’. el-maktab byisakkir es-saa‘a wahde.
lines.id: Unfortunately not. The office closes at one.
lines.literal: to-the-regret no. the-office it-closes hour one.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: طَيِّب. مُمْكِن حَدَا تَانِي يْجِيبْهُن عَنِّي؟
lines.id: OK. Can someone else bring them for me?
lines.literal: good. possible someone other he-brings-them for-me?

lines.speaker: اَلْمُوَظَّف:
lines.id: No, you have to come in person.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: OK. I'll talk to the teacher.

lines.speaker: اَلْمُوَظَّف:
lines.text: أَحْسَن شِي. وْلَازِم مَا تْتَأَخَّر أَكْتَر.
lines.baca: ahsan shi. w laazim ma tit’akhkhar aktar.
lines.id: That's best. And you mustn't put it off any longer.
lines.literal: best thing. and must not you-delay more.

lines.speaker: اَلْمُوَظَّف:
lines.id: Your permit runs out in a week.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: يَا اللَّه! يِسْلَمُوا، رَح إِجِي بُكْرَا بَكِّير.
lines.baca: ya alla! yislamu, rah iji bukra bakkiir.
lines.id: Oh my God! Thanks, I'll come first thing tomorrow.
lines.literal: O God! may-they-be-safe, will I-come tomorrow morning.

notes: **All three are followed by the bare verb, without b-.** Just like after بَدِّي and رَح. The form is لَازِم تِجِي، مُمْكِن أَسْأَل، فِيني أَجِيب. This is the fourth and last rule of its kind; once you've got it, the whole A1 verb system is complete.

**The word لَازِم doesn't change across the eight persons.** It's one fixed word, and only the verb changes: لَازِم أَرُوح (I have to go), لَازِم تْرُوح (you have to go), لَازِم يْرُوح (he has to go). كَان لَازِم means "should have."

**The word مُمْكِن has two jobs.** Asking permission, it means "may": مُمْكِن أَسْأَل؟ As a statement, it means "maybe": مُمْكِن يِجِي بُكْرَا ("maybe he'll come tomorrow"). The tone tells them apart.

**⚠️ The word فِيني means "I can" in the sense of being able or having time, and it's not a verb.** The forms are فِيني، فِيك، فِيكِي، فِيه، فِيهَا، فِينَا، فِيكُن، فِيهُن — the same endings again. The negative is مَا — for example مَا فِيني.

**The word بِقْدَر also means "can," but leans toward physical ability.** مَا بِقْدَر إِمْشِي means "I can't walk" (a bad leg, say), while مَا فِيني إِمْشِي is more "I can't make it" or "it's not possible." The line is blurry, and native speakers often swap them.
**To forbid with لَازِم, put مَا after it.** The form is لَازِم مَا تْتَأَخَّر ("you mustn't be late"). It's firmer than لَا تْتَأَخَّر from unit 9, and usually means there are consequences.

grammars.title: Four words and how they differ
after: ⚠️ Look carefully at the first row: **مِش لَازِم doesn't mean "forbidden," it means "don't have to."** مِش لَازِم تِجِي means "you don't have to come," not "you mustn't come" — the same trap as English "must not" versus "don't have to." To forbid, use مَمْنُوع or لَازِم مَا.
The words فِيني and بِقْدَر both change with the person, but in different ways: فِيني takes possessive endings, while بِقْدَر is an ordinary verb with the b- prefix that follows the unit 8 pattern.

grammars.title: The word فِيني in eight forms
after: ⚠️ The word فِيه clashes with فِيه, meaning "there's … in it," from unit 12. Position tells them apart: followed by a verb, it means "he can"; followed by a noun or on its own, it means "in it."
The phrase فِيك تْسَاعِدْنِي؟ ("can you help me?") is one of the most useful sentences in this whole book. Learn it as a whole, and use it whenever you're stuck.

blocks.text: The word مَعْلِيش works both ways, and that's what makes it so useful. Said by the person saying no, it means "sorry." Said by the person being turned down, it means "never mind." It's also used to comfort someone in trouble, and in that sense it's one of the warmest words in Levantine Arabic.

blocks.title: Prohibitions you'll see on signs
items: **A sign reading مَمْنُوع التَّدْخِين** *mamnuu‘ et-tadkhiin* means "no smoking."
**A sign reading مَمْنُوع التَّصْوِير** *mamnuu‘ et-taṣwiir* means "no photography" — and it's serious near government buildings and military posts throughout the Levant.
**A sign reading مَمْنُوع الدُّخُول** *mamnuu‘ ed-dukhuul* means "no entry."

blocks.text: The phrase كَان لَازِم expresses regret for something not done — exactly like English "should have." It's often used to blame yourself gently, and the reply is almost always مَعْلِيش.

blocks.title: Helper words that round off this unit
items: The word لَيش *lēsh* means "why," and the answer starts with لَإِنّ *la’inn* ("because"): لَيش مَا جِيت؟ لَإِنّي كِنِت تَعْبَان.
The word شَخْصِيًّا *shakhṣiyyan* means "personally, in person" — a word you'll hear in every government office.
The word لَلْأَسَف *lal-asaf* means "unfortunately." It softens any refusal, and using it makes you sound much more polite.
You have to bring your passport.
